Confident in recovery especially in bottlenecks as earnings and FCF accumulate, calling it more the Great AI Deleveraging of 2026 than demand destruction.
text:
It think it's stupid that "AI Bubble" gets used over and over. In infra names you have: 

- 1-3x fwd P/E memory companies from Samsung to $ESMT. With HBM players now having hyperscaler multi-year price floor LTAs. 

- Optical companies like $POET traded -$97M under net cash. Valuing the operating business very negatively, not even at $0. 

- While AI companies with larger premiums continue to record demand over the next 3-5 years. Such as the new $20B LTAs signed w/ $COHR to $5B LTAs signed w/ $LITE. 

Can someone in the media honestly see negative EV high-beta optical companies, where 2 years of burnrate would still value the company below $0.  

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

Many of these names are extremely profitable today... 

But obviously there's other elements inside the theme, such as: 

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously. 

But everything gets grouped into one with the boogyman of "leverage" or "debt". 

Yes, valuations can compress or correct from macro, potential regulatory uncertainty, or potential capex reductions. 

But for the companies physically powering the AI buildout, it looks more like the Great AI Deleveraging of 2026... 

Than anything like fundamental demand destruction.

As more earnings come out and free cash

text:

If you look at how $NVDA CEO describes CPO, Jensen states scale up is increasing optical volumes by 15x. $LITE and $COHR are quantifying that by describing $5-$20B agreements spanning 3-5 years out.

Having this question, and not talking about Ayar, O-Net, Poet, or ELS partnerships. Then redirecting the question to near term pluggables seems off.

The vision also needs work, “communications and sensing” semi company is very unexciting.

It’s technically true, but there’s no vision being communicated on being the next $40B optical giant or what Sivers is going to be in the next 5 years that would attract long term holders.

The core valuation Sivers gets is from optical opportunities, I also personally disagree that it’s helpful to loop back to former cellular relationships when talking about future $GFS volumes

I disagree when you portray the company as “small” when Sivers 100m CW DFB capacity is coming online, alongside large foundry partners.

Which is a material % of the world’s annual laser capacity.

Investors want to hear about future economic opportunities and how you fill the gap with more qualifications during a bottleneck.

Sivers has a tremendous opportunity for CPO/NPO/Pluggables but I’m afraid it’s not being communicated properly. 

It’s understandable here since EETimes is more technical oriented, but I hope this messaging gets communicated better in the next earnings

text:
Counterpoint on $MRVL / $LITE acqusition:

- "Every buyer that competes with Marvell will want a second, independent laser source".

They identify $SIVE / Scintil Photonics as new CW / ELS capacity, with names like $CRDO as potential partners of Sivers.

- "With Lumentum sold out for years, the overflow goes to whoever has merchant capacity"

Already said this before, but we'll likely see some incentive to diversify laser sourcing. 

Sivers was cited here, and comes online with 100M lasers / external foundry capacity (2:1 external/internal target). 

To demonstrate the sheer scale on that, $AAOI exit 2026 laser capacity target was roughly ~24M/year (but different blend). 

- "Module makers move upstream" was also another second order effect. 

 $JBL as one example is now heavily competing with the combined Lumentum + Marvell.... There's other players like $SMTC that are explicitly doing M&A for expanding laser capacity.

I don't think the overall AI valuation crash is representative of individual company strength in the optical sector.

There's very compelling opportunities in the laser bottleneck in the upcoming year that I believe markets are mispricing.

$GRAB

Grab had an exceptional Q3.

- Raised EBITDA guide from 45% growth to 60% growth YoY
- Total quarterly active advertisers on self-serve platform grew 39% YoY, and average spend of these advertisers grew 13% YoY
- Adjusted FCF now $533M, doubling YoY
- Financial services is now profitable

Network effects compounding with operating leverage is the simple thesis, unfortunately oil has been the headwind but this was an outstanding quarter for the company.

text:
Meta is lining up an AI bond deal of at least $20B, split across dollars and euros. Bloomberg reported at about 12:16 PM ET that Citi and Morgan Stanley are holding investor calls today and tomorrow. That makes Meta the third hyperscaler in high-grade today, after Oracle and Alphabet, and it comes on top of last month's shelf registration and forward stock sale. The things to watch are how much extra spread Meta has to pay, whether its CDS widens, and whether demand holds up after Oracle's slide. (Bloomberg)

Oracle's $10B bond and $10B stock sale still hadn't priced as of 3:30 PM ET. The stock is down about 8.6% at around $126.

Ratings. Fitch kept Oracle at BBB and said it doesn't expect much more capital raising. Moody's affirmed its rating and kept the negative outlook.
Credit. The 6.85% 2066 bonds fell more than 1.2 points, and five-year CDS is still around 296 bp.
Next. Final pricing should be in the next run's update. (Yahoo Finance)

 Scott see below (debunking the relationship between s and p eps and s and p prices).
